findings.title: Module boundary violation: browse CLI imports host config via dynamic absolute path
findings.description: browse/src/cli.ts dynamically imports hosts/index.ts using path.resolve(__dirname, '..', '..', 'hosts', 'index.ts'). This creates a hidden cross-module dependency from the browse subsystem (which compiles to a standalone binary) into the hosts/ registry. It bypasses the module system, breaks in compiled binaries (where __dirname points into $bunfs), silently falls back to a hardcoded convention path on failure, and couples browse to the gstack monorepo layout. The browse binary should be self-contained per its design as a 'persistent Chromium daemon'.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) extract host globalRoot resolution into a small data file (e.g., hosts/globals.json) that browse can read, (b) accept the globalRoot as a CLI argument from the calling skill, or (c) move the --local pair-agent flow into a separate gstack-level CLI that legitimately depends on hosts/. The current dynamic path import is an architectural shortcut that defeats the binary's portability.

findings.title: God object: BrowserManager has 40+ public methods spanning 8 unrelated concerns
findings.description: BrowserManager in browser-manager.ts is a classic god object. It owns: lifecycle (launch/close/handoff), tab management, ownership/multi-agent isolation, dialog handling, cookie tracking, viewport/UA, watch mode, ref maps, snapshot diffing, frame context, two-tier CDP mutex, headed mode patches, anti-bot stealth scripts, plist patching, icon copying, and SSE-style disconnect callbacks. The mutex acquisition logic alone (acquireTabLock/acquireGlobalCdpLock) is non-trivial concurrency code mixed with file system I/O for icon rebranding. This violates SRP and makes the class very hard to test in isolation — every test must stub a 1500+ line surface.
findings.recommendation: Extract focused collaborators: (1) TabRegistry (pages/sessions/ownership), (2) CdpMutex (two-tier locking), (3) HeadedBrandingService (plist/icon patching), (4) StateSerializer (saveState/restoreState), (5) WatchSession (watch* methods). BrowserManager would become a thin facade that composes these. This is a multi-PR refactor — start with TabRegistry since it's the most leaked.

findings.title: server.ts is a 1500+ line monolith mixing routing, business logic, and lifecycle
findings.description: browse/src/server.ts is a single file containing: HTTP routing for ~20 endpoints, dual-listener tunnel management, ngrok integration, SSE streaming for activity + inspector, command dispatch with security pipeline (scope/domain/tab/rate/audit/wrapping), idle/parent-process watchdogs, signal handlers, terminal-agent IPC, cookie picker integration, welcome page serving, and start/shutdown sequencing. The makeFetchHandler factory alone is ~700 lines with deeply nested if-chains for path matching. There is no router abstraction — adding a route requires editing the megafunction.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a minimal route table (Map<{method, path}, handler>) and split handlers into route modules: routes/auth.ts (/connect, /pair, /token, /agents, /sse-session, /pty-session), routes/command.ts (/command, /batch), routes/inspector.ts, routes/activity.ts, routes/tunnel.ts, routes/static.ts (/health, /welcome, /file). Keep makeFetchHandler as the surface filter only. handleCommandInternal already shows the pattern is feasible — apply it to routing.

findings.title: Inconsistent host adapter pattern: registry array hardcodes imports, no Protocol/interface enforcement
findings.description: hosts/index.ts hardcodes 10 imports and an ALL_HOST_CONFIGS array. Adding a new host requires editing this central registry — a closed-for-extension pattern. There is no interface/protocol shown that enforces what each host config exports beyond a HostConfig type alias; consistency across claude/codex/factory/etc. depends on convention. The comment 'Adding a new host: create hosts/myhost.ts, import here, add to ALL_HOST_CONFIGS' acknowledges the manual coupling.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) use a directory-scan + dynamic import pattern at build time (codegen a registry from hosts/*.ts), or (b) keep the explicit array but add a runtime validator in tests that asserts every HostConfig has the same shape (validateHostConfig schema). The latter is lower-effort and catches drift immediately. Document the HostConfig contract more explicitly with required vs optional fields.

findings.title: Resolver registry lacks namespacing and grouping despite 50+ entries from 13+ source modules
findings.description: scripts/resolvers/index.ts collects 50+ resolver functions into a flat Record<string, ResolverFn>. The placeholders (SLUG_EVAL, COMMAND_REFERENCE, DESIGN_METHODOLOGY, INVOKE_SKILL, etc.) span many domains — preamble, browse, design, testing, review, learnings, gbrain, question-tuning, make-pdf — but live in a single flat namespace. There is no way to discover which placeholders are valid for a given skill template, no precedence rules, no validation that the source modules export what RESOLVERS claims, and the inline import block is ~20 lines of imports.
findings.recommendation: Group resolvers by domain into nested namespaces (e.g., RESOLVERS.design.METHODOLOGY) or split into separate files per category and merge at the top level. Add a buildtime test that asserts every key in RESOLVERS has a corresponding template placeholder in at least one skill template, and vice versa, to catch drift. Consider a registry pattern where each module self-registers rather than the central index.ts importing all of them.

findings.title: browse-client SDK distribution model trades versioning correctness for portability
findings.description: browse/src/browse-client.ts documents that 'each browser-skill ships a sibling copy at <skill>/_lib/browse-client.ts'. This means every skill bundles its own SDK copy, frozen at authoring time. While the comment justifies this ('version drift is impossible'), it actually inverts the problem: a daemon protocol change breaks every existing skill silently because the SDK copies don't update. There is no versioning handshake between SDK and daemon — only HTTP status codes. With 50+ skills, a wire protocol bump becomes a fanout migration.
findings.recommendation: Add a ProtocolVersion header to every /command request and have the daemon reject incompatible versions with a clear upgrade message. Bake the SDK version into the per-skill copies at generation time. Provide a `$B skill upgrade <name>` command that re-copies the bundled SDK. Without these, the 'frozen SDK' design will rot as the daemon evolves.

findings.title: Orphan/dead code shipped: ~150 lines of ripped functionality referenced in comments
findings.description: server.ts contains multiple 'ripped' comment blocks referencing removed functionality (sidebar agent, chat queue, ChatEntry interfaces, agentProcess, agentStatus, sidebarSession, processAgentEvent, killAgent, listSessions, getTabAgent, agentHealthInterval, sidebar model router, /sidebar-tabs, /sidebar-chat, /sidebar-agent endpoints). The comments serve as institutional memory but pollute the file and indicate incomplete cleanup of a major architectural change. browser-manager.ts also has 'TabAgentState interfaces; chatBuffer, chatBuffers, sidebarSession...' references.
findings.recommendation: Move the 'ripped' decision rationale into a CHANGELOG.md or ADR (Architecture Decision Record) and delete the inline comment tombstones. The git history preserves the code. Right now, every reader of server.ts re-encounters these graveyard markers, increasing cognitive load. If retention is desired for navigation, a single reference like `// See ADR-014 for sidebar-agent removal` is sufficient.

findings.title: Inverted dependency: lib/worktree.ts uses runtime require() into hosts/ to break ESM cycle
findings.description: lib/worktree.ts uses `const { getExternalHosts } = require('../hosts/index')` inside the create() method. This is a CommonJS-style lazy require inside an otherwise ESM module, suggesting a deliberate workaround for a circular dependency or load-order issue between the platform library (lib/) and the hosts/ registry. Mixing import + require() patterns is a code smell that hides cycle-breaking logic.
findings.recommendation: Refactor to either (a) inject getExternalHosts as a constructor parameter so worktree.ts has no compile-time dependency on hosts/, or (b) move the host-list resolution outside WorktreeManager.create() into the calling test harness. Alternatively, if there's no actual cycle, just promote it to a top-level ESM import. The current require() obscures the dependency from static analysis tools and tree-shakers.

findings.title: make-pdf orchestrator referenced in PLAN but file not provided; verify orchestrator boundary
findings.description: The plan focus lists make-pdf/src/orchestrator.ts as a key file for assessing module boundaries with browse/, but only make-pdf/src/cli.ts was provided. The CLI uses lazy `await import('./orchestrator')` and `await import('./setup')` which is good for cold-start latency but also a code-splitting boundary worth verifying. Cannot fully assess orchestrator-level layering without the file. CLI-side error mapping (BrowseClientError, PagedJsTimeout, ENOENT) is well-structured and exit-code-driven.
findings.recommendation: Confirm orchestrator.ts only imports browse via the documented browse-client SDK and not via the daemon's internal modules. The current CLI structure (commands.ts → cli.ts → lazy orchestrator) is healthy.

findings.title: Tunnel command allowlist drift risk between TUNNEL_COMMANDS and canDispatchOverTunnel
findings.description: server.ts defines TUNNEL_COMMANDS (a Set) and canDispatchOverTunnel() (a pure gate using that set). The set is exported and also referenced inline in /command tunnel-surface checks. The risk is that future tunnel-allowed commands need updates in three places: TUNNEL_COMMANDS, the dispatch error message ('Tunnel commands: [...TUNNEL_COMMANDS].sort().join'), and downstream documentation. There's no test coverage shown that asserts every command in TUNNEL_COMMANDS exists in ALL_COMMANDS or in one of READ/WRITE/META command sets.
findings.recommendation: Add a startup assertion or test that every entry in TUNNEL_COMMANDS is a known command (i.e., appears in READ_COMMANDS ∪ WRITE_COMMANDS ∪ META_COMMANDS after canonicalization). This catches typos and removed commands. Also consider deriving the error hint message from TUNNEL_COMMANDS at module-load time, not per-request.

findings.title: Auth token leaked via /health endpoint without origin restriction
findings.description: The /health endpoint returns the daemon's root AUTH_TOKEN unconditionally when in headed mode, and to any caller whose Origin header starts with 'chrome-extension://'. The Origin header is client-controlled in non-browser contexts (curl, fetch from any process on the host), and any local process on 127.0.0.1 can read it. Comments in the code acknowledge this as 'a separate concern (v1.1+ TODO)'. A malicious local process or compromised browser extension could fetch the token and gain root capability over the daemon, including ability to mint scoped tokens, run JS in arbitrary tabs, read cookies, etc. CWE-522: Insufficiently Protected Credentials. OWASP A07:2021.
findings.recommendation: Remove the token from /health entirely. Use a separate authenticated bootstrap endpoint that requires either a one-time exchange code (similar to setup_key flow) or a filesystem-protected handoff (read token from ~/.gstack/.auth.json with 0600 perms, which the code already writes). Origin header is not a security boundary against local processes.

findings.title: Telemetry-ingest accepts arbitrary installation_id without authentication or rate limiting
findings.description: The Supabase telemetry-ingest edge function accepts events with client-supplied installation_id (up to 64 chars), gstack_version, os, and writes them via the anon key. There is no authentication, no per-installation rate limit, and no signature verification. An attacker can poison the telemetry table at scale, inflate weekly_active counts, manipulate top_skills/top_versions in /community-pulse, or spam crash_clusters. The 50KB/100-event-per-batch caps only slow this. CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity. CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits.
findings.recommendation: Add a per-IP rate limit (e.g. 100 events/min) via Supabase rate limiting or an edge proxy. Consider HMAC-signed events using a key the gstack client derives from installation_id (still defeatable but raises bar). At minimum, log source IP for forensic analysis and add a CAPTCHA-like proof-of-work for high-volume submitters.

findings.title: Insufficient lock file content validation (TOCTOU on lock file PID parsing)
findings.description: acquireServerLock() in cli.ts reads the lock file, parseInts the contents, and checks if the PID is alive. An attacker (or a colliding test) could write a fake PID matching an unrelated alive process (e.g., pid 1) into the lock file, and the lock would be considered held forever, blocking server startup. Inverse: a stale lock could be removed and concurrent starts could race. CWE-367: TOCTOU Race Condition.
findings.recommendation: Use fcntl/flock-style advisory locks where available, or include a lock file timestamp + content signature so a stale lock is detected by age. The wx flag handles the basic atomic create case but the recovery path (read PID + recreate) is racy.

findings.title: PTY session token transmitted in JSON response body in addition to HttpOnly cookie
findings.description: The /pty-session endpoint returns the freshly-minted ptySessionToken in the JSON response body so the extension can pass it via Sec-WebSocket-Protocol. The code's own comment acknowledges this is required because browsers don't allow custom headers on WebSocket from JS. However, this means the token sits in JS-accessible memory in the page that called fetch() — defeating the HttpOnly protection of the parallel cookie. Any XSS in the extension UI page (sidepanel) would be able to exfiltrate the token. CWE-522.
findings.recommendation: The current design accepts this trade-off explicitly. Mitigations: (1) Ensure Sidebar UI has strict CSP with no inline scripts and no unsafe-eval. (2) Keep the 30-min token TTL short (already done). (3) Verify the WebSocket upgrade also validates a per-connection challenge so a stolen token alone is not enough. (4) Document the threat model clearly so future changes don't widen the surface.

findings.title: Activity stream filterArgs may miss password fields with non-standard names
findings.description: filterArgs() in activity.ts redacts fill values when the selector matches /password|passwd|secret|token/i. Sites using 'pin', 'pwd', 'auth-code', '2fa', 'otp', 'mfa' or non-English language fields (e.g., 'mot-de-passe') will leak credentials to the activity stream. The activity stream is exposed via SSE to any holder of the SSE session cookie (which is bound to root token bootstrap, so risk is bounded but the data is still persisted in the in-memory ring buffer). CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information.
findings.recommendation: Expand the regex to cover common credential field names: /password|passwd|pwd|secret|token|pin|otp|mfa|2fa|auth.?code|cvv|ssn|social/i. Better: redact ALL fill values by default and only allow plain values when the selector explicitly matches a known-safe pattern (e.g., 'search', 'query', 'comment'). Defense in depth: also match by input type=password attribute via pre-fill metadata.

findings.title: Browser anti-detection patches inject permissive scripts that could be abused
findings.description: launchHeaded() injects an addInitScript that overrides navigator.plugins, navigator.languages, and navigator.permissions.query, plus deletes window.cdc_* and __webdriver* variables. These patches make the browser appear non-automated. Legitimate use case (avoiding bot blocks for the user's own browsing) but deliberately defeats site-side automation detection — websites' Terms of Service may prohibit this. Not a security vuln per se but worth documenting the trade-off.
findings.recommendation: Document the anti-detection behavior in user-facing docs and obtain user consent at install time. Consider an opt-out flag (BROWSE_NO_STEALTH=1) for users who want strict default Playwright behavior.

findings.title: Skill spawn token TTL not enforced against orphaned tokens on crash
findings.description: spawnSkill() mints a scoped token via mintSkillToken, then in finally{} calls revokeSkillToken. If the parent process is SIGKILLed mid-spawn, the token registry's in-memory state may be lost but if it's persisted (token-registry.ts handles serialization), the token could outlive the spawn. The spawn ID + skill name binding limits blast radius but a determined attacker who learns the token + port could replay until the registry is rebuilt.
findings.recommendation: Ensure mintSkillToken sets an absolute expiresAt (timeout + 30s slack as documented) and that validateScopedToken always checks expiry on read. Periodically purge expired tokens from the registry. On daemon restart, drop all skill-spawned tokens (only persist root + paired-agent tokens).

findings.title: Syntax error in cli.ts disconnect handler — invalid JSON.stringify body
findings.description: In handlePairAgent's disconnect path, the body of fetch contains a stray `domains,` line inside JSON.stringify that references an undeclared variable in this scope, breaking compilation. This indicates either dead code from a bad merge or a broken disconnect flow that never actually runs/compiles. Critical because it would prevent the binary from building.
findings.recommendation: Remove the orphaned `domains,` line from the JSON.stringify({ command: 'disconnect', args: [] }) call. Add a build/typecheck step (tsc --noEmit) to the test script to catch syntax errors before commit.

findings.title: server.ts is a 1500+ line god module with mixed concerns
findings.description: browse/src/server.ts handles HTTP routing, auth, tunnel management, SSE streaming, inspector state, PTY handshake, audit logging, idle/parent watchdogs, signal handling, port discovery, command dispatch, and lifecycle — all in one file. The makeFetchHandler closure alone spans hundreds of lines with deeply nested route handlers. This makes it hard to test individual routes in isolation (the PLAN explicitly flags this concern) and creates merge-conflict pressure across unrelated features.
findings.recommendation: Extract route groups into modules: routes/auth.ts (/connect, /token, /pair), routes/inspector.ts, routes/sse.ts, routes/batch.ts, routes/tunnel.ts. Keep server.ts as the wiring layer (<300 lines). This enables direct unit testing of each route without standing up Bun.serve.

findings.title: BrowserManager class spans 800+ lines with too many responsibilities
findings.description: BrowserManager owns browser lifecycle, tab management, dialog handling, ownership tracking, viewport/UA state, watch mode, headed/handoff state, CDP locks (two-tier mutex), state save/restore, ref maps, frame context, cookie tracking, Chromium binary patching for branding, and stealth init scripts. The launchHeaded() method alone embeds DOM-injection scripts, plist patching, icon copying, anti-bot evasion, user-agent detection, and tab adoption. This violates SRP and makes the class very hard to test or refactor.
findings.recommendation: Split responsibilities: extract HeadedLauncher (plist+icon+UA), AntiDetectionScripts (stealth init), TabOwnership, CdpLockManager, StateSnapshotter. Keep BrowserManager focused on Browser/Context/Page lifecycle. Improves testability — currently almost everything requires a real Chromium.

findings.title: Custom YAML frontmatter parser is fragile and untested for edge cases
findings.description: browser-skills.ts implements a hand-rolled YAML subset parser (parseFrontmatterFields, collectArgsList, collectStringList) for SKILL.md files. The author notes 'Anything more exotic should use a real YAML library — not in Phase 1 scope.' Hand-rolled parsers tend to silently misparse: nested quotes, escapes, multiline strings, tabs vs spaces. As skills proliferate this becomes a class of latent bugs and security issues (a malformed frontmatter could cause silent skip per the catch-and-continue in listBrowserSkills).
findings.recommendation: Replace with `yaml` npm package (or js-yaml). Add property-based tests with adversarial frontmatter inputs. Until then, surface parse errors at validation time rather than swallowing them — currently malformed skills are silently skipped, which is a debuggability nightmare.

findings.title: Flakiness risk in tests dependent on PTY/CDP/live network
findings.description: PLAN explicitly flags flakiness risk in PTY/CDP/live-network tests. The package.json shows --retry 2 on eval suites, which masks flakes rather than fixing them. Auto-retry is a smell: failing tests get re-run until they pass, hiding real intermittent bugs. The 30s/8s/15s wait windows in cli.ts (MAX_START_WAIT) and 5s ngrok probes also create timing-dependent test assertions.
findings.recommendation: Track per-test flake rate; tests that fail on first run >5% of the time should be quarantined and fixed. Replace network-dependent tests with localhost stubs (BROWSE_TUNNEL_LOCAL_ONLY=1 already exists for this — extend the pattern). Mock time-based polling with deterministic clocks in unit tests.

findings.title: Documentation file inventory listed but contents not provided for verification
findings.description: The PLAN lists 13+ documentation files (README, ARCHITECTURE, CONTRIBUTING, DESIGN, ETHOS, BROWSER, SKILL, AGENTS, CLAUDE, TODOS, docs/skills.md, docs/domain-skills.md, docs/ADDING_A_HOST.md) which represents an unusually thorough documentation set for a project of this complexity. The breadth (multiple agent-host guides + design philosophy docs + ADRs in docs/designs/) signals strong commitment to documentation. However, only source code was provided, so this assessment focuses on inline/code-level documentation.
findings.recommendation: No action — note for context that the project has invested heavily in narrative documentation (ETHOS, DESIGN, ARCHITECTURE) beyond standard README/CONTRIBUTING coverage, which is a positive signal.

findings.title: Strong file-level docstrings across the codebase
findings.description: Nearly every source file opens with a substantive header comment explaining purpose, architecture, and key invariants. Examples: server.ts has Architecture/State sections; cli.ts documents the Flow; activity.ts has an ASCII diagram of subscriber flow; buffers.ts documents the ring-buffer with a diagram; browser-manager.ts documents crash handling and context-recreation semantics; browse-client.ts documents auth resolution and trust model. This is well above industry norm.
findings.recommendation: Maintain this standard. Consider extracting the header comments into a doc-generator pipeline so module overviews surface in API reference output.

findings.title: Inline rationale comments preserve non-obvious decisions
findings.description: Many comments capture *why* a non-obvious choice was made, not just *what* the code does. Examples: cli.ts line 78-82 explains why Windows hard-fails without server-node.mjs; server.ts line 268-282 documents the SIGTERM handling rationale across modes; browser-manager.ts has a long block explaining anti-bot stealth patches; cdp lock acquisition has rationale for tab vs global locks. These prevent future regressions from well-meaning refactors.
findings.recommendation: Continue this practice. Consider tagging especially load-bearing comments with a marker like `// LOAD-BEARING:` to make them easier to find during code review.

findings.title: References to ripped/deleted features may confuse new readers
findings.description: Several files contain comments describing features that were 'ripped' (sidebar-agent.ts, chat queue, /sidebar-* endpoints, tab-agent multiplexing). While the historical context is useful, comments like 'sidebar-agent.ts spawn was here. Ripped alongside the chat queue' and '// ─── Sidebar agent / chat state ripped ──────────────' assume reader familiarity with prior versions. New contributors won't know what 'the chat queue' was.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) move historical context to a CHANGELOG/MIGRATION doc and replace inline comments with a one-line pointer, or (b) link the rip-comments to a specific PR/commit hash so curious readers can dig deeper. Currently 8+ such comments exist across server.ts, cli.ts, and browser-manager.ts.

findings.title: CLI help text duplicates command knowledge between cli.ts and server.ts
findings.description: browse/src/cli.ts contains a hardcoded help string (~40 lines, around the `if (args.length === 0 || args[0] === '--help'`) listing commands and snapshot flags. Meanwhile, server.ts has generateHelpText() that auto-generates from COMMAND_DESCRIPTIONS + SNAPSHOT_FLAGS (the canonical source of truth). These will drift — adding a new command to commands.ts will update server.ts help but not CLI help. The CLI help even references flags like `-D/--diff`, `-a/--annotate`, `-C/--cursor-interactive` that must be kept in manual sync with snapshot.ts.
findings.recommendation: Have the CLI fetch help text from the running server (or share a small static module) so commands documented in COMMAND_DESCRIPTIONS auto-propagate. Alternative: write a build-time check that fails if the CLI help string doesn't match generateHelpText() output.

findings.title: Public exported functions in browse-client.ts have docstrings; consumer onboarding is well-served
findings.description: browse-client.ts is the SDK skill-script authors import. Its module header explains distribution model, auth resolution order, and trust boundaries; BrowseClient methods are grouped by section (Navigation, Reading, Interaction, Snapshot+screenshot) with section dividers. resolveBrowseAuth() has a clear contract documented. This is the right level of detail for an SDK consumed by agent-authored code.
findings.recommendation: No action. Consider adding one or two `@example` blocks to BrowseClient methods (e.g. snapshot, click) to give skill authors copy-paste starting points without reading SKILL.md fixtures.

findings.title: Edge function source files lack module headers
findings.description: supabase/functions/community-pulse/index.ts, telemetry-ingest/index.ts, and update-check/index.ts each open with 2-3 line comments naming the function but don't document: HTTP contract (expected request shape), response schema, rate-limit assumptions, or deployment requirements (env vars, table dependencies). community-pulse references community_pulse_cache, telemetry_events, crash_clusters, installations tables and a K_ANON constant — the rationale is good (inline at K_ANON) but the schema dependencies are not catalogued.
findings.recommendation: Add module headers documenting: required Supabase tables, required env vars (SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, SUPABASE_ANON_KEY, GSTACK_CURRENT_VERSION), expected request body shape, and response schema. ~30 mins per function.

findings.title: Some public exports lack JSDoc on parameters and return types
findings.description: Public exports like `extractTabId` (cli.ts), `resolveServerScript` (cli.ts), `canDispatchOverTunnel` (server.ts), `parseSkillFile` (browser-skills.ts), `validateSkillName` (browser-skill-write.ts) have brief inline doc comments, but most don't use @param/@returns tags. For an SDK-style codebase where these are consumed by tests and downstream skills, structured tags help IDE tooltips and doc generators. Functions like `BrowserManager.checkTabAccess` have rich prose docs — that's the bar.
findings.recommendation: Add @param and @returns where the function is publicly exported and the parameter list is non-trivial (3+ params or any optional param). Group similar exports with a single sweep — ~15 functions across cli.ts, server.ts, and the skill modules.

findings.title: Frontmatter parser in browser-skills.ts is documented as 'tiny tuned subset'
findings.description: parseFrontmatterFields() in browser-skills.ts is correctly flagged as a YAML subset implementation with 'Anything more exotic should use a real YAML library — not in Phase 1 scope.' This is good honest documentation. However, the supported subset is described informally; users authoring SKILL.md files won't know what fails until parseSkillFile throws. Frontmatter examples in docs/skills.md (not provided here) should explicitly show the supported syntax.
findings.recommendation: Either expand the inline doc to include 1-2 worked examples of supported syntax, or cross-reference the doc that has them (e.g. `// See docs/skills.md § Frontmatter for examples`). Reduces the support burden when someone uses an unsupported YAML feature.

findings.title: TODOS.md presence suggests roadmap is documented
findings.description: The file list includes TODOS.md alongside ARCHITECTURE.md and DESIGN.md. Combined with comments like '(v1.1+ TODO)' in server.ts and references to plan files (CEO plan, sec-wave v1.6.0.0), the project appears to maintain a forward-looking roadmap that ties code comments to planning docs. This is unusual and positive for contributor onboarding.
findings.recommendation: If TODOS.md is auto-generated or manually maintained, ensure it is dated/owner-tagged so stale items can be retired. Consider linking inline 'TODO' comments to TODOS.md entries by ID.

findings.title: Adding-a-host doc presence is well-aligned with the registry pattern
findings.description: hosts/index.ts documents the host-add flow inline ('Adding a new host: create hosts/myhost.ts, import here, add to ALL_HOST_CONFIGS'). docs/ADDING_A_HOST.md exists as a longer-form guide. The two-tier docs (inline pointer + dedicated guide) is the right pattern for an extension point that contributors will hit. Verify the inline comment matches what ADDING_A_HOST.md actually instructs.
findings.recommendation: Cross-link them explicitly: change the inline comment to `Adding a new host: see docs/ADDING_A_HOST.md (TL;DR: create hosts/myhost.ts, import here, add to ALL_HOST_CONFIGS).`

findings.title: Unused 'domains' parameter leftover in server.ts disconnect handler
findings.description: In cli.ts around the disconnect command's HTTP body construction, there's a stray `domains,` followed by `command: 'disconnect'`. This appears to be a copy-paste leftover from the pair-agent body — `domains` is not in scope here. While not strictly a documentation issue, it indicates the surrounding code lacks the comment that would have flagged this as 'don't include domains for disconnect — the body shape diverges intentionally.'
findings.recommendation: Remove the stray `domains,` or, if intentional, document why disconnect ships a domains key. Looks like a real bug surfaced by missing inline rationale.

findings.title: No lock file ecosystem verification — bun.lock listed but not validated
findings.description: The plan mentions bun.lock but its freshness vs package.json cannot be verified from provided code. Bun lock files require periodic regeneration to match package.json declarations, especially when caret ranges (^) allow drift. Recommend CI validation that `bun install --frozen-lockfile` succeeds.
findings.recommendation: Add CI step `bun install --frozen-lockfile` to ensure bun.lock matches package.json. Document lockfile-update policy in CONTRIBUTING.md.

findings.title: Caret-ranged production dependencies allow silent minor/patch drift
findings.description: All runtime dependencies use caret ranges (^4.1.0, ^1.7.0, ^7.0.0, ^18.0.2, ^1.58.2, ^24.40.0). With caret ranges + a lock file, installs are reproducible, but `bun install` without --frozen-lockfile in dev environments can pull in newer minors. For a tool that ships compiled binaries (browse/dist/browse, make-pdf/dist/pdf) bundling these deps, drift could introduce regressions between developer machines.
findings.recommendation: Either pin exact versions for production deps that ship in compiled binaries, or document that lockfile is the source of truth and enforce --frozen-lockfile everywhere (CI + local build script).

findings.title: Heavy ML dependency (@huggingface/transformers) in runtime deps with unclear usage
findings.description: @huggingface/transformers ^4.1.0 is declared as a runtime dependency. This package is large (typically 100MB+ with model loading code) and pulls in onnxruntime-web. No usage is visible in the analyzed code (browse/server.ts, design/cli.ts, make-pdf/cli.ts, etc.). If unused or only used in optional code paths, this bloats install size for all users and increases attack surface.
findings.recommendation: Audit actual usage of @huggingface/transformers. If only used by an optional feature, move to optionalDependencies or lazy-load via dynamic import with a separate install path. If unused, remove entirely.

findings.title: Two competing browser automation libraries — playwright and puppeteer-core both as runtime deps
findings.description: Both `playwright` ^1.58.2 and `puppeteer-core` ^24.40.0 are declared as runtime dependencies. server.ts and browser-manager.ts use playwright exclusively (chromium.launch, BrowserContext). Carrying both inflates install size significantly (Playwright alone ships browser binaries) and doubles CVE exposure surface. puppeteer-core does not appear used in any analyzed file.
findings.recommendation: Verify puppeteer-core is actually imported anywhere; if not, remove it. If used in a non-shown file, document why both are needed or migrate to a single library.

findings.title: xterm v5 declared with imprecise major-only range
findings.description: devDependency `"xterm": "5"` uses a bare major version, which resolves to any 5.x.x. xterm has been deprecated in favor of @xterm/xterm scoped package since 2024. The `vendor:xterm` script copies xterm.js + xterm-addon-fit into extension/lib/, so any change in xterm's published files affects shipped extension assets.
findings.recommendation: Pin xterm to a specific version (e.g., `"xterm": "5.3.0"`) or migrate to the new @xterm/xterm + @xterm/addon-fit scoped packages which receive ongoing maintenance.

findings.title: Vendored xterm assets copied at build-time without integrity verification
findings.description: The `vendor:xterm` build script copies node_modules/xterm/lib/xterm.js into extension/lib/ as part of the build. These vendored files are then loaded into the Chrome extension which talks to the daemon over WebSocket. There's no SRI hash, version pin to a commit/tag, or signature check. A compromised xterm publish (typosquat/maintainer takeover) would land directly into the shipped extension.
findings.recommendation: Either (1) commit the vendored xterm files directly so they're git-reviewed, (2) add SRI hash verification in the vendor:xterm script, or (3) pin xterm to an exact version + audit each upgrade.

findings.title: External Deno edge functions pin major version via esm.sh URL
findings.description: Supabase edge functions import from `https://esm.sh/@supabase/supabase-js@2` with no minor/patch pin. esm.sh resolves @2 to whatever latest 2.x is at request time, meaning two cold-starts can run different code. A compromised supabase-js publish would propagate to all edge function invocations immediately. Same issue across community-pulse/index.ts, telemetry-ingest/index.ts, update-check/index.ts.
findings.recommendation: Pin to a specific version: `https://esm.sh/@supabase/supabase-js@2.45.4`. Better: use Deno's `deno.lock` or import map to lock all transitive imports.

findings.title: @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk pinned to exact prerelease version
findings.description: @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk is pinned to exact version 0.2.117 (no caret), which is good for reproducibility but the SDK is in 0.x prerelease and likely unstable. There's no upgrade strategy visible. Comments in code reference 'sidebar-agent.ts ripped' suggesting recent churn.
findings.recommendation: Add a CHANGELOG entry process for SDK version bumps. Consider adding Renovate/Dependabot config to surface new releases for review without auto-merging.

findings.title: Bun runtime version range is permissive (>=1.0.0)
findings.description: engines.bun is `>=1.0.0` which spans nearly two years of Bun releases including known stability issues in early 1.x. The codebase uses recent Bun-specific APIs (Bun.spawn, Bun.serve, Bun.file, AbortSignal.timeout) and platform-specific fixes (Windows compatibility comments reference recent Bun versions).
findings.recommendation: Tighten to `"bun": ">=1.1.0"` or whichever minimum version was tested. Document the supported Bun range in README.

findings.title: No SBOM generation or supply-chain attestation in build pipeline
findings.description: The build script compiles binaries that bundle all dependencies (`bun build --compile`) and ships them as `browse/dist/browse`, `make-pdf/dist/pdf`, etc. No SBOM (CycloneDX/SPDX) is generated alongside, and no attestation (SLSA, sigstore) is created. Users installing the binaries cannot easily verify what dependencies are bundled or check for CVEs without re-installing the source.
findings.recommendation: Add `bun pm pkg` or `cyclonedx-bom` step to the build script to generate sbom.json. Consider GitHub artifact attestations for releases.

findings.title: Synchronous fs.appendFileSync blocks event loop on every flush
findings.description: flushBuffers() runs every 1 second and uses fs.appendFileSync three times (console, network, dialog logs). With 50,000-entry CircularBuffers, each flush can serialize and write large blocks synchronously, blocking the Bun event loop and stalling all in-flight HTTP commands during the write. The 'async' marker on flushBuffers() is misleading — there are no awaits.
findings.recommendation: Replace fs.appendFileSync with fs.promises.appendFile (or Bun.write with append). The flushInProgress guard already prevents concurrent flushes, so an async write is safe. This removes the 1-Hz event-loop stall under heavy logging.

findings.title: Unbounded response body buffering for network capture
findings.description: In browser-manager.ts wirePageEvents(), every requestfinished event calls `await res.body()` which loads the full response body into memory just to compute its byte length. For pages that download large assets (videos, PDFs, large JSON), this allocates the full payload (potentially hundreds of MB) per request only to discard it. With BROWSE_HEADED, the user can navigate to anything — a single video stream can OOM the daemon.
findings.recommendation: Use the Content-Length response header when present, or fall back to a size cap (e.g., skip body() for responses where headers indicate >1MB; or read response.headers()['content-length']). Never download the body solely to count bytes.

findings.title: Activity buffer toArray() copies 1000 entries on every getActivityAfter()
findings.description: getActivityAfter() in activity.ts calls activityBuffer.toArray() (allocates a 1000-element array) then filters it with a linear scan. Every SSE client connection and every poll triggers this. Multiple sidebar/extension clients amplify the cost. Since entries are inserted with monotonic IDs, a binary search on the ring buffer would suffice.
findings.recommendation: Add a method to CircularBuffer that returns entries with id > afterId without materializing the full array — binary search the head-relative position, then iterate from there. Alternatively, only materialize the slice past afterId.

findings.title: JSON.parse on every state-file read inside hot path
findings.description: Several handlers (/tunnel/start, BROWSE_TUNNEL bootstrap) call fs.readFileSync(config.stateFile, 'utf-8') + JSON.parse + writeFileSync + renameSync to update tunnel info. While these are administrative paths, the same pattern (sync read + parse + write) happens in cli.ts during ensureServer() polling loops at 100-200ms intervals. On Windows where syscalls are slower, this measurably extends startup.
findings.recommendation: Cache parsed state in cli.ts startServer() polling loop instead of re-reading and re-parsing every 100ms. Compare mtime first; only re-parse if the file changed.

findings.title: PDF orchestrator code referenced in plan was not provided — cannot evaluate concurrency
findings.description: The PLAN focuses on make-pdf/src/orchestrator.ts and make-pdf/src/render.ts (PDF rendering pipeline concurrency) and scripts/resolvers/composition.ts (preamble generation cost on hot paths), but the analyzed_code section did not actually include those files. Cannot make findings on the rendering pipeline concurrency or resolver composition cost without source.
findings.recommendation: Re-run analysis with make-pdf/src/orchestrator.ts, make-pdf/src/render.ts, scripts/resolvers/composition.ts, and test/helpers/benchmark-runner.ts contents included.
